INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
Amicus curiae Stephen I. Vladeck is the Agnes
Williams Sesquicentennial Professor of Federal
Courts at Georgetown University Law Center.  He is
one of the nation’s leading scholars on federal
jurisdiction, the separation of powers, and the role of
federal courts in redressing constitutional violations.
Professor Vladeck’s scholarly work bears directly
on the question presented, including publications
examining the historical roots of Bivens v. Six
Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of
Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388 (1971).  His scholarship has
detailed the interaction between Bivens and the
Westfall Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2679, as well as related
doctrinal developments in Ziglar v. Abbasi , 582 U.S.
120 (2017); Hernández v. Mesa (Hernández II) , 589
U.S. 93 (2020); and Egbert v. Boule , 596 U.S. 482
(2022).  Professor Vladeck also was counsel of record
for the petitioners in Hernández II.
Professor Vladeck submits this brief to explain
why Bivens and Carlson v. Green, 446 U.S. 14 (1980),
were proper exercises of the Court’s federal common
lawmaking authority to provide remedies, including
money damages, for violations of a person’s
constitutional rights.  The brief also addresses why
neither Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins , 304 U.S. 64
(1938), nor the Court’s later Bivens decisions provide
a basis for treating Carlson as obsolete.

1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in part,
and no person other than amicus and his counsel made a
monetary contribution intended to fund the preparation or
submission of this brief.

2
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
As respondent correctly explains, this case
presents a straightforward application of Carlson.
See Watanabe Br. 14-15.  Respondent alleges that a
federal prison official was deliberately indifferent to
his serious medical needs in violation of the Eighth
Amendment—the same constitutional claim this
Court recognized as actionable under Bivens more
than four decades ago.  The Ninth Circuit correctly
held that respondent’s claim does not present a “new
context” under Ziglar v. Abbasi, 582 U.S. 120 (2017),
and the historical and doctrinal foundations of
Carlson confirm that result.  See Watanabe v. Derr ,
115 F.4th 1034 (9th Cir. 2024).
The Court should not allow Carlson to atrophy into
irrelevance through the “obsolescence” framework
that the United States urges.  See Amicus Br. of
United States 23-28.  Carlson rests on a distinct
common-law tradition of judge-made remedies for
constitutional violations—a tradition most clearly
articulated in Justice Harlan’s concurrence in Bivens
and later confirmed by Carlson itself.
Decisions that have cabined Bivens remedies often
equate them to an implied statutory cause of action,
but the analogy is inapt.  Unlike a statutory remedy,
a constitutional damages action vindicates rights that
no other body of law supplies.  Eliminating that action
would leave many constitutional violations without a
remedy, raising serious questions about the
constitutionality of the Westfall Act.
Erie does not foreclose the judiciary’s centuries-old
authority to award damages for constitutional
violations.  If Erie is not an obstacle to the continued

3
expansion of qualified immunity—a judicially created
doctrine—then it is no obstacle to a federal commonlaw remedy that holds federal officers accountable for
violating a person’s constitutional rights.
Finally, nothing in Hernández II or any other
post-Carlson decision supports treating Carlson as
obsolete.  To the contrary, this Court has repeatedly
reaffirmed the three established Bivens contexts
while declining to extend them further.  Following the
same path here should lead to a decision affirming the
Ninth Circuit’s judgment and allowing respondent’s
claim to proceed.
ARGUMENT
I. Bivens And Carlson Were Proper Exercises Of The
Court’s Federal Common-Law Authority.
A federal court exercising jurisdiction over a
constitutional claim has the traditional common-law
authority to fashion an appropriate remedy for the
violation alleged.  See Bivens , 403 U.S. at 398-401
(Harlan, J., concurring in the judgment).  That
authority does not depend on express congressional
authorization; courts have long awarded equitable
relief without legislative authorization, and there is
no sound reason to recognize the propriety of a
prospective equitable remedy but not a retrospective
damages remedy.  Id. at 404-05.  When equitable
relief cannot redress a constitutional injury, damages
might be the only appropriate relief.  Id. at 407-10.
Properly understood, then, Bivens did not infer a
cause of action from the statutory signals of
congressional intent.  Rather, Bivens is rooted in the
federal courts’ traditional common-law authority to

4
provide an appropriate remedy for when a federal
officer violates a person’s constitutional rights.
A. Federal Courts Possess Traditional Remedial
Authority Over Constitutional Claims.
“[W]here federally protected rights have been
invaded, it has been the rule from the beginning that
courts will be alert to adjust their remedies so as to
grant the necessary relief.”  Bell v. Hood , 327 U.S.
678, 684 (1946).  The federal judicial power to provide
a private damages remedy in a suit alleging
constitutional harms “hardly has been doubted for
over two hundred years.”  Nixon v. Herndon, 273 U.S.
536, 540 (1927).  Since the Founding, “the traditional
way” for redressing constitutional harms caused by
federal officers “was by subjecting them to liability for
common-law torts.”  Hernández II, 589 U.S. at 110.
Under these historical traditions, once a federal
court has jurisdiction over a constitutional claim, it
also has common-law authority to determine an
appropriate remedy—whether equitable or legal.  See
Bivens, 403 U.S. at 405-07 & n.6 (Harlan, J.,
concurring in the judgment).  Congress recognized
this traditional judicial authority when granting
federal district courts original jurisdiction over “all
civil actions arising under the Constitution, laws, or
treaties of the United States.”  28 U.S.C. § 1331.
That jurisdictional grant itself does not prescribe
a damages remedy.  But federal courts are not
powerless to award damages for a constitutional
violation merely because Congress has not expressly
authorized a remedy.  See Bivens, 403 U.S. at 403-06
(Harlan, J., concurring in the judgment).  It would
make little sense to conclude that Congress gave

5
federal courts jurisdiction over a category of claims
that the courts are powerless to redress.
Section 1331’s jurisdictional grant brings the
constitutional claim before federal courts, which in
turn have authority to determine whether damages
are necessary and appropriate to redress the alleged
violation.  See Bivens , 403 U.S. at 400-01, 405-07
(Harlan, J., concurring in the judgment).  The
relevant inquiry is not whether Congress intended to
create a cause of action but whether awarding
damages is “necessary” or “appropriate” to vindicate
the constitutional deprivation.  Id. at 404-07.
The settled availability of equitable relief without
express statutory authorization confirms that the
judiciary’s traditional injury-redressing power does
not infringe on the legislative branch or otherwise
violate the separation of powers.  Federal courts have
long exercised equitable authority to restrain
unconstitutional federal action without a statute
expressly authorizing that relief.  See Bivens , 403
U.S. at 400, 404-05 (Harlan, J., concurring in the
judgment) (citing cases).  So the absence of express
statutory authorization does not mean federal courts
lack authority to provide an appropriate remedy for
constitutional violations.  See id.  at 404-06.  The
historical distinctions between law and equity might
affect which remedy is appropriate, but they do not
speak to the existence of traditional judicial authority
to award both types of relief.  See id. at 406; see also
Armstrong v. Exceptional Child Ctr., Inc. , 575 U.S.
320, 327 (2015) (recognizing the historical availability
of equitable relief against unlawful official action);
Osborn v. Bank of United States , 22 U.S. (9 Wheat.)
738, 838-46, 849-50, 870-71 (1824) (sustaining

6
nonstatutory relief); The Apollon, 22 U.S. (9 Wheat.)
362, 365-67, 372-74, 379 (1824) (sustaining damages
against a federal officer); Little v. Barreme , 6 U.S.
(2 Cranch) 170, 178-79 (1804) (same).
In short, nothing in the historical record supports
accepting judicially fashioned prospective equitable
relief while disfavoring or rejecting damages.  The
absence of express statutory authorization does not,
by itself, foreclose federal courts from fashioning an
appropriate damages remedy for a constitutional
violation when prospective equitable relief is
inappropriate or inadequate.  Damages provide the
traditional means of compensating an invasion of a
legally protected interest and are available when
necessary or appropriate to vindicate a constitutional
violation.  And in selecting an appropriate remedy for
the violation, courts exercise judicial authority; they
do not arrogate legislative power.  See Marbury v.
Madison, 5 U.S. (1 Cranch) 137, 177 (1803).
These traditional remedial powers are not cabined
to the specific Fourth Amendment context of Bivens.
Individual instances of discrimination, lawenforcement overreach, or other constitutional
misconduct are often “difficult to address except by
way of damages after the fact.”  Abbasi, 582 U.S. at
144.  Whenever prospective equitable relief cannot
undo a constitutional violation, damages might be the
only remedy capable of vindicating the right.  That
holds true when a federal officer’s deliberate
indifference has already caused a prisoner’s pain and
physical harm: prospective relief may secure
adequate medical care going forward, but only
damages can compensate the constitutional injury
already inflicted.  See Carlson, 446 U.S. at 16 & n.1,

7
18-23; see also Watanabe Br. 40-41 (citing cases).
When those circumstances exist, the practical choice
is “damages or nothing.”  Bivens, 403 U.S. at 410
(Harlan, J., concurring in the judgment).
B. Davis And Carlson Confirm The Judiciary’s
Authority To Redress Constitutional Violations
With Damages Awards.
Davis and Carlson apply Bivens’s remedial
framework outside the context of the Fourth
Amendment to rights secured by the Fifth and Eighth
Amendments.  Each decision confirms that damages
are an appropriate remedy for a constitutional
violation when Congress has not displaced the
remedy and no special factors counsel hesitation.  See
Davis v. Passman , 442 U.S. 228, 245-49 (1979); see
also Carlson, 446 U.S. at 18-23; Bivens, 403 U.S. at
396-97 (opinion of the court); id. at 404-07 (Harlan, J.,
concurring in the judgment).
Davis illustrates that framework in action.
Shirley Davis alleged that Congressman Otto
Passman terminated her employment because she
was a woman, thereby violating the equal protection
component of the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process
Clause.  Davis, 442 U.S. at 230-31, 234-35.  The Court
treated the constitutional right and the available
remedy as distinct questions.  It first asked whether
the Fifth Amendment secures the asserted right and
then asked whether damages provide an appropriate
remedy for the alleged violation.  See id. at 239-48.
Damages were appropriate because (1) courts had
substantial experience adjudicating analogous
employment-discrimination claims, (2) reinstatement
was unavailable because Passman no longer served in

8
Congress, and (3) no alternative judicial relief could
redress Davis’s injury.  Id. at 245 & n.23.  For Davis,
as for Bivens, the remedial choice was “damages or
nothing.”  Id. at 245 (quoting Bivens, 403 U.S. at 410
(Harlan, J., concurring in the judgment)).
Carlson applied the same framework in the Eighth
Amendment prison context.  The claim alleged that
federal prison officials were deliberately indifferent to
a prisoner’s serious medical needs.  446 U.S. at 16 &
n.1, 17-18.  The Court asked whether special factors
counseled hesitation or Congress had expressly
declared another remedy to be a substitute for
constitutional recovery.  Id. at 18-19.  Because neither
limitation applied, the Court held that the Federal
Tort Claims Act complements, rather than displaces,
the Bivens remedy against the prison officials.  Id. at
19-20.  The Court added that the Bivens remedy
provides greater deterrence, permits punitive
damages and a jury trial, and supplies a uniform
federal rule of liability.  Id. at 20-23.
Carlson thus treats congressional action as
relevant only to whether the judiciary’s traditional
remedial authority has been displaced—not whether
such authority exists in the first instance.
II. Constitutional Remedies Are Not Implied
Statutory Causes Of Action.
This Court’s recent decisions limiting the scope of
Bivens and its progeny often analogize to the rule
preventing courts from finding implied causes of
action in federal statutes.  See, e.g., Abbasi, 582 U.S.
at 132-35; Hernández II , 589 U.S. at 100-01.  That
analogy is misplaced.  It detracts from the traditional

9
constitutional role of courts and has sown more
confusion than clarity.
The false analogy between implied statutory
causes of action and Bivens remedies stems most
directly from Justice Scalia’s concurrence in
Correctional Services Corp. v. Malesko , 534 U.S. 61
(2001).  Justice Scalia described Bivens as “a relic of
the heady days in which this Court assumed commonlaw powers to create causes of action—decreeing them
to be ‘implied’ by the mere existence of a statutory or
constitutional prohibition.”  Id. at 75 (Scalia, J.,
concurring) (emphasis added).  That seed has since
overgrown into a “general reluctance to extend
judicially created private rights of action,” Jesner v.
Arab Bank, PLC , 584 U.S. 241, 264 (2018)—a
formulation that wrongly collapses the distinction
between statutory and constitutional remedies.
Generally speaking, federal courts should not
imply statutory remedies because doing so
undermines the rights—and limitations on those
rights—created by Congress.  See Alexander v.
Sandoval, 532 U.S. 275, 286-87 (2001); cf. Abbasi, 582
U.S. at 135 (explaining that “separation-of-powers
principles are or should be central to the analysis”).
But constitutional rights exist independently of—and
sometimes despite—a federal statute.  The judiciary
does not invade the legislature’s purview when it
redresses constitutional violations.  If anything,
separation of powers at times requires  courts to
recognize and provide a constitutional remedy
precisely because Congress has not provided one.
Indeed, before Carlson in 1980, the Court had
become “chary” of reading implied damages remedies

10
into statutes.   Transamerica Mortg. Advisors v.
Lewis, 444 U.S. 11 (1979).  Yet that chariness in the
statutory context did not stop the Court one year later
from extending the constitutional Bivens remedy to
the Eighth Amendment context in Carlson.
Justice Scalia’s description of Bivens as a “relic” of
“heady days” is also misplaced.  He was referring to
the “ancien regime” discussed in Sandoval, 532 U.S.
at 287.  That regime involved cases from the 1960s
and 1970s in which courts went beyond their
constitutional purview and found remedies implied in
statutes.  Those decisions provide no reason to fear
implied constitutional remedies, which are consistent
with—if not required by—the separation of powers.
See Martin H. Redish, Constitutional Remedies as
Constitutional Law , 62 B.C. L. Rev. 1865, 1920-22
(2021) (explaining why converging statutory and
constitutional remedies is improper).  Moreover, the
origin of Bivens is not “heady” but firmly grounded in
centuries of federal common law, see supra Part I, and
the origin of the country itself, see Bivens, 403 U.S. at
397 (“‘The very essence of civil liberty certainly
consists in the right of every individual to claim the
protection of the laws, whenever he receives an
injury.’” (quoting Marbury, 5 U.S. at 163)).
The consequences of denying a constitutional
remedy are far more severe than the consequences of
denying a statutory one.  When a constitutional
remedy is unavailable, a troubling question arises
that this Court has sidestepped at least once:  If a
plaintiff is not entitled to a Bivens remedy, is the
Westfall Act unconstitutional because its prohibition
of state-law tort claims against federal employees
eliminates access to the courts?  See Pet. for Cert. at i,

11
Hernández v. Mesa  (June 15, 2018) (No. 17-1678);
Hernández v. Mesa , 587 U.S. 1025 (2019) (mem.).
The Act preempts essentially all state-tort suits
against federal officers for wrongful acts done while
acting in their official capacity, but it carved out an
“explicit exception for Bivens claims.”  Hui v.
Castaneda, 559 U.S. 799, 807 (2010) (discussing
28 U.S.C. § 2676(b)(2)(A)).  Eliminating Bivens claims
would create absolute immunity for federal officers,
leaving victims of constitutional wrongs without a
legal remedy.  See Watanabe Br. 29-30, 45-46.
III. Erie Does Not Foreclose Federal Common-Law
Remedies.
This Court last upheld a Bivens claim almost five
decades ago in Carlson.  Later cases characterize
Bivens as a superseded, “ancien regime.”  Abbasi, 582
U.S. at 131 (quoting  Sandoval, 532 U.S. at 287); see
also  Hernández II , 589 U.S. at 99.  That
characterization overlooks the robust common-law
tradition for remedying federal officer misconduct.
See supra Part I; see also Br. of Carlos M. Vázquez &
Anya Bernstein as Amici Curiae in Supp. of Pet’rs 2,
Hernández II, 589 U.S. 93 (2020) (No. 17-1678).  It
also misapplies Erie.
Erie’s holding that “[t]here is no federal general
common law,” 304 U.S. at 78, was directed at a
specific issue—the practice by which federal courts
sitting in diversity applied “general common law” that
varied from state law.  Hernández II, 589 U.S. at 100
(quoting Erie, 304 U.S. at 78); see also Carlos M.
Vázquez, Bivens and the Ancien Régime, 96 Notre
Dame L. Rev. 1923, 1924, 1931-32 (2021).  Before
Erie, this general common law “was neither federal

12
law nor state law” but “had features of both.”
Vázquez, supra, at 1931.  In finding that this
“in-between status no longer existed,” id., Erie did not
hold that federal courts lack common lawmaking
authority or the authority to fashion remedies for
when federal officials violate a person’s constitutional
rights.  Instead, Erie required federal courts to decide
whether the applicable law would be “upgrade[d]” to
federal law or “downgrade[d]” to state law.  Id.
Recognizing that federal common law remained
very much viable, on the same day the Court decided
Erie, it also held that “federal common law” would
govern disputes between states.  Hinderlider v. La
Plata River & Cherry Creek Ditch Co. , 304 U.S. 92,
110 (1938).  And as the Court has explained many
times since Erie, federal common law has continued
to govern in areas of “peculiarly federal concern.”
Boyle v. United Techs. Corp. , 487 U.S. 500, 504-05
(1988) (identifying areas of “uniquely federal
interests” warranting displacement of state law by
“federal common law”); Clearfield Tr. Co. v. United
States, 318 U.S. 363, 366-67 (1943) (recognizing
federal common law for commercial paper issued by
the United States); Texas Indus., Inc. v. Radcliff
Materials, Inc., 451 U.S. 630, 641 (1981) (identifying
“areas where federal common law applies” such that
“the creation of a right to contribution may fall within
the power of the federal courts”); Collins v. Virginia,
584 U.S. 586, 607 (2018) (Thomas, J., concurring)
(noting the contexts in which the Court has continued
to fashion federal common law after Erie).
The question in Bivens was whether the
traditional common-law right to sue federal officers
for official misconduct, which held “in-between

13
status” before Erie, Vázquez, supra, at 1931, was
available as a federal cause of action for damages.  In
adopting what became known as the Bivens remedy,
the Court regarded the remedy as “hardly . . . a
surprising proposition” because “[h]istorically,
damages have been regarded as the ordinary remedy
for an invasion of personal interests in liberty.”
Bivens, 403 U.S. at 395 (citations omitted).  “In the
context of suits against Government officials,
damages have long been awarded as appropriate
relief” stretching back to the “early Republic,” and
“damages against federal officials remain an
appropriate form of relief today.”  Tanzin v. Tanvir ,
592 U.S. 43, 49 (2020); see also Richard H. Fallon, Jr.,
Constitutional Remedies: In One Era and Out the
Other, 136 Harvard L. Rev. 1300, 1308 (2023)
(“[S]haping the right-remedy relationship is a crucial
lawmaking function that has historically been shared
between Congress and the courts, especially the
Supreme Court.”).  Thus, “ Bivens can be best
understood as providing a federal right to sue that
builds on the common past and tailors the common
law suit for use in a post- Erie world.”  Vázquez &
Bernstein Amicus Br. 22.
But as “this Court’s general reluctance to extend
judicially created private rights of action” increased
in the modern era, Jesner v. Arab Bank, PLC , 584
U.S. 241, 264 (2018), the Court has largely gutted
Bivens.  In Hernández II, the Court acknowledged the
historical tradition of judge-made damages remedies
but, for the first time, relied on Erie to dismiss the
relevance of that tradition.  589 U.S. at 99-100.
Because of Erie and “the demise of federal general
common law,” Justice Alito wrote for the  majority,

14
“federal courts today cannot fashion new claims in the
way they could before 1938;” rather, “a federal court’s
authority to recognize a damages remedy must rest at
bottom on a statute enacted by Congress . . . and no
statute expressly creates a Bivens remedy.”  Id. at
100-01 (citations omitted).  The lone justification
offered for that proposition was the rejection of
implied statutory causes of action in Sandoval.  See
id. (citing Sandoval, 532 U.S. at 286-87).  But as
explained above, that justification rests on an inapt
analogy.  See supra Part II.
Although Hernández II was correct in recognizing
that Erie changed the framework for federal common
law, its use of Erie to restrict “a federal court’s
authority to recognize a damages remedy” to cases in
which a “statute expressly creates a Bivens remedy”
is materially overstated.  589 U.S. at 101.  Erie
required courts to justify applying federal rather than
state common law; the decision did not require courts
to abandon their common-law power to redress
constitutional violations.  Bivens, 403 U.S. at 400-02
(Harlan, J., concurring in the judgment); see also
Vázquez & Bernstein Amicus Br. 22 (“In the pre-Erie
era, courts . . .  had not been particularly careful about
pinning down the locus of common law rights to sue
federal officers for official misconduct.”).
Hernández II and other post-Bivens cases also fail
to explain why the Court would take decades to
acknowledge such a monumental implication of Erie.
Even the  Solicitor General, on behalf of the Bivens
respondents, when arguing against a judicially
created federal damages remedy, did not read Erie to
foreclose the power of federal courts to fashion
common law.  See Br. of Resp’ts 19-20,  Bivens v. Six

15
Unknown Named Agents of the Fed. Bureau of
Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388 (1971) (No. 301), 1970 WL
122211, at *19-20 (noting that “the creation by the
federal courts of common-law rights” are “few and
restricted” because “we are not in the free-wheeling
days antedating” Erie (citation omitted)).
Even if Erie had the impact the majority claimed
in Hernández II , neither decision explains why
foreclosing federal judicial power to fashion remedies
would be limited to damages suits but not equitable
suits.  See, e.g., Armstrong v. Exceptional Child Ctr.,
Inc., 575 U.S. 320, 327 (2015) (“The ability to sue to
enjoin unconstitutional actions by state and federal
officers is the creation of courts of equity, and reflects
a long history of judicial review of illegal executive
action, tracing back to England.”).  What justification
does Erie provide for reconfiguring federal judgemade remedies so that they are available in cases
seeking prospective relief but (almost) nonexistent
when plaintiffs seek retrospective relief?
The Court’s modern Bivens jurisprudence
provides no answer to that question.  Instead,
although the Court has scaled back Bivens actions as
a “disfavored” judicial activity, Abbasi, 582 U.S. at
135 (quoting Ashcroft v. Iqbal , 556 U.S. 662, 675
(2009)), it has continued to identify circumstances in
which judicially made remedies are permissible and
even necessary.
The qualified-immunity doctrine is one of the most
evident examples.  The Court has fashioned modern
qualified-immunity doctrine with no suggestion that
doing so runs afoul of Erie.  In Pierson v. Ray , 386
U.S. 547 (1967), the Court assumed Section 1983

16
incorporated “common-law immunities” and held that
officials acting in “good faith” can raise qualified
immunity as a defense.  Id. at 554, 557 (discussing
42 U.S.C. § 1983); see also Imbler v. Pachtman , 424
U.S. 409, 418 (1976) (reasoning that Section 1983 “is
to be read in harmony with general principles of tort
immunities and defenses rather than in derogation of
them”).  Likewise, in Harlow v. Fitzgerald , 457 U.S.
800 (1982), the Court held that federal executive
officials enjoy immunity from damages liability
unless their actions violate clearly established
constitutional rights that “a reasonable person would
have known.”  Id. at 818.  That standard had no
statutory basis; Congress did not create it.  See
William Baude, Is Qualified Immunity Unlawful? ,
106 Calif. L. Rev. 45, 47, 51-77 (2018).
Indeed, the Harlow standard “conferred a broader
immunity from damages than most officials had ever
received in suits at common law.”  Fallon, supra, at
1331.  And the Court has continued to expand
qualified immunity for federal officials without
legislative action, imposing a standard of ever-greater
specificity in the “clearly established” inquiry, see
Ashcroft v. al-Kidd , 563 U.S. 731, 741 (2011), and
raising pleading standards in Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678—
all without addressing how this expansion rests on
statutory interpretation rather than judicial common
lawmaking.  See Kisela v. Hughes, 584 U.S. 100, 121
(2018) (Sotomayor, J., dissenting) (criticizing the
Court’s “one-sided approach to qualified immunity” in
recent decisions); Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 157 (Thomas, J.,
concurring in part and concurring in the judgment)
(noting “growing concern” with the Court’s “qualified
immunity jurisprudence”).

17
If Erie does not forbid federal courts from creating
a judge-made immunity doctrine that shields federal
officers from liability, it also does not forbid federal
courts from fashioning remedies to hold such officers
accountable.  Although the Court has voiced disdain
for “creat[ing] new federal common law,” Sosa v.
Alvarez-Machain, 542 U.S. 692, 746 (2004) (Scalia, J.,
concurring in part and concurring in the judgment), it
exercises precisely that authority when developing
qualified-immunity doctrines.  See Crawford-El v.
Britton, 523 U.S. 574, 611-12 (1998) (Scalia, J.,
dissenting) (“We find ourselves engaged, therefore, in
the essentially legislative activity of crafting a
sensible scheme of qualified immunities for the
statute we have invented—rather than applying the
common law embodied in the statute that Congress
wrote.”).  The only difference is directional: qualified
immunity protects the federal officer; a Bivens action
protects the victim of a federal officer’s misconduct.
As Justice Scalia wrote for the Court in Boyle,
“civil liability of federal officials for actions taken in
the course of their duty” is an area of “peculiarly
federal concern” such that “the scope of that liability
is controlled by federal law” and “warrant[s] the
[judicial] displacement of state law.”  487 U.S. at 505.
If that is so, then the power to shape the terms of such
liability necessarily includes the cause of action, the
defenses to it, and the remedies for it.  See Fallon,
supra, at 1360 (“If taken at face value, the modern
Supreme Court’s separation of powers rationale for
rejecting Bivens actions would also condemn other
forms of federal common lawmaking . . . including the
recognition of federal common law defenses against
state law causes of action.”).

18
IV. Hernández II Provides No Basis For Rendering
Carlson Obsolete.
Nothing in Hernández II supports treating
Carlson as obsolete.  Hernández II did not reconsider,
much less overrule, any established application of
Bivens—nor of Davis or Carlson.
In Hernández II , a U.S. Border Patrol agent
standing in the United States fired across the
international border and killed a Mexican national
standing in Mexico.  589 U.S. at 96 -97.  The Court
described the case as a request “to extend Bivens” to
a cross-border shooting.  Id. at 96.  It held that the
claim arose in a new context because it differed in
meaningful respects from the claims previously
recognized under Bivens.  See id. at 102-03.  Looking
beyond the constitutional provisions invoked, the
Court considered it “glaringly obvious” that the crossborder setting presented a new context.  Id. at 103.
The Court’s reasons for declining to recognize a
remedy were specific to that international setting.  It
emphasized that the cross-border shooting was “by
definition an international incident” affecting the
interests of the United States and Mexico.
Hernández II, 589 U.S. at 104-06.  It separately
concluded that the conduct of the Border Patrol
agents stationed at the border bears a “clear and
strong connection to national security” and that the
risk of undermining border security counseled
hesitation.  Id. at 107-09.  The Court also relied on
Congress’s treatment of claims arising from injuries
inflicted outside the United States.  Id. at 109-13.
Taken together, those considerations led the Court to

19
leave to the political branches the task of recognizing
a remedy for cross-border claims.
Those context-specific grounds do not reach
Carlson.  An Eighth Amendment claim against
federal prison officials for deliberate indifference to a
federal prisoner’s serious medical needs implicates
none of the foreign relations, national security, border
security, or extraterritorial concerns on which
Hernández II  relied.  Nothing in Hernández II
suggests that a damages remedy would be
unavailable if the facts of Bivens recurred without
any asserted interference with national security.
So Carlson remains on solid footing, and
respondent here pursues the same type of remedy for
the same type of misconduct: federal prison officials’
deliberate indifference to a federal prisoner’s serious
medical needs.  See Watanabe Br. 14-15.  The
constitutional right asserted, the alleged misconduct,
the custodial setting, and the category of defendants
all place respondent’s claim comfortably within
Carlson’s established context.
The new-context inquiry asks whether a claim
differs “in a meaningful way” from the claims this
Court has recognized in prior cases.  Abbasi, 582 U.S.
at 139.  It does not require the later claim to reproduce
every factual detail of the prior case.  Rather, the
Court focuses on differences relevant to the propriety
of a judicial remedy, including the constitutional right
at issue, the officers’ legal mandate, the extent of
judicial guidance, and the risk of intrusion into the
function of the political branches.  Id. at 139-40.
Variations in the severity of the injury, the course of

20
treatment, or the precise medical condition do not
alter that remedial context.  Those matters bear on
whether respondent can factually establish deliberate
indifference to a serious medical need, not on whether
his claim extends Bivens beyond Carlson.  See Farmer
v. Brennan, 511 U.S. 825, 834, 837 (1994).
Hernández II confirms that distinction.  Although
the Court described its understanding of a new
context as “broad,” it still required a meaningful
difference from the context of claims in which a
damages remedy has been recognized.  Hernández II,
589 U.S. at 102-03.  Respondent’s claim presents no
such meaningful difference with Carlson.
Treating every factual variation as a new context
would confine Carlson to its precise facts and deprive
it of precedential force.  But the governing inquiry
asks whether the differences are meaningful, not
whether the facts are identical.  See Abbasi, 582 U.S.
at 139-40; Hernández II, 589 U.S. at 102-03.  Because
respondent’s claim falls within the remedial context
Carlson established, applying Carlson here follows
this Court’s precedent.  It does not extend Bivens.
Hernández II declined to extend Bivens, but it did
not overrule any of its established applications.  The
majority applied the new-context and special-factors
framework and refused to recognize a remedy for the
distinct cross-border claim before it.  Hernández II,
589 U.S. at 102-14.  Justice Thomas, joined by Justice
Gorsuch, wrote separately to urge the Court to
consider “discarding the Bivens doctrine altogether.”
Id. at 114 (Thomas, J., concurring).  The majority did
not take that step.  Declining to recognize a remedy
in a new context leaves existing precedent in place;

21
treating an established application as obsolete
eliminates the precedent itself.  Thus, Hernández II,
a decision declining to extend Bivens, cannot and did
not do the work of overruling Carlson.
The Court has continued to identify Carlson as one
of the three cases in which it recognized a damages
remedy under the Constitution.  See Hernández II ,
589 U.S. at 99; Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 131.  Although
later decisions have declined to extend those
precedents to new contexts, the Court has identified
“powerful reasons” to retain Bivens.  Abbasi, 582 U.S.
at 134-35.  Hernández II followed that same
structure.  It identified the three established contexts
before asking whether the cross-border claim was
meaningfully different from them.  See Hernández II,
589 U.S. at 102.
This Court does not discard a directly controlling
precedent merely because later decisions have
questioned its reasoning or limited its reach.  See
Halliburton Co. v. Erica P. John Fund, Inc. , 573 U.S.
258, 266 (2014) (“Before overturning a long-settled
precedent, . . . we require ‘special justification,’ not
just an argument that the precedent was wrongly
decided.” (quoting Dickerson v. United States,  530
U.S. 428, 443 (2000))).  If Carlson no longer governs
the Eighth Amendment context that it recognized, it
governs nothing.  That result would overrule Carlson
in substance while avoiding the discipline of doing so
expressly.  See Watanabe Br. 31-32.
Applying Carlson to respondent’s claim, by
contrast, respects both decisions and principles of
stare decisis.  It preserves the established remedy
recognized in Carlson without extending Bivens

22
beyond that context.   And it correctly acknowledges
that, just as Erie left in place the power of federal
courts to fashion federal common-law defenses in
suits against federal officers, it likewise preserved the
power of federal courts to fashion federal common-law
remedies in those same cases.
CONCLUSION
The Court should affirm the judgment of the Ninth
Circuit.
